The core operator 'superstar absence elasticity' (E_s) is derived from hedonic pricing theory applied to NBA ticket markets. It measures how much the willingness-to-pay for a game drops when a superstar is absent. This is modeled as a linear function of the change in ticket prices on a secondary marketplace. The welfare loss function (\mathcal{L}) aggregates these individual impacts into a macroeconomic measure. Market normalization adjusts E_s by log(M) to reflect that larger markets are less sensitive to superstar absences. These primitives form a dual structure: one rooted in behavioral economics (demand elasticity), the other in aggregate economic loss. Failure modes include non-linear demand curves, exogenous shocks, and misalignment of secondary market data with primary market behavior. The system exhibits robustness under stable market conditions but fails under sudden policy changes or unexpected player availability.
